extracted.intended_audience: high-school students preparing for the ACT Writing Test / college applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for the optional 40-minute ACT argumentative essay: how it is scored, the four scoring domains, and practical tips for planning, writing, and preparing.

rubrics_metrics.name: How the ACT Writing Test is Scored
rubrics_metrics.description: Each ACT writing test is graded by two different readers, who give the essay a score between 1 and 6 in four areas. The two readers’ scores are averaged, and the test receives a final score between 2 and 12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writing test is scored separately from the ACT composite. You will receive domain scores (2–12) for each of the four domains (sum of the two readers), and a single overall score (2–12) found by averaging the four domain scores. If the two readers’ scores differ by more than a point, a third reader evaluates the essay to resolve the discrepancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas and Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: This domain concerns the ability to generate productive ideas and engage critically with multiple perspectives on the given issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your essay should have a clear and focused thesis. Use your thesis to consider at least two of the provided perspectives. Don’t just state simple agreement or disagreement with perspectives—fully explore the strengths and weaknesses of each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development and Support
rubrics_metrics.description: This domain concerns the ability to discuss ideas, offer rationale, and bolster an argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific examples to illustrate larger ideas and clearly explain why the examples are relevant. Each new idea you introduce should build on previous ideas and deepen the support for your thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization
rubrics_metrics.description: This domain concerns the ability to organize ideas with clarity and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On a large scale, have an introduction (with thesis), several body paragraphs, and a conclusion. On a smaller scale, body paragraphs should include topic sentences and move from more general arguments to the use of specific examples. All information about the same idea(s) should be grouped together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language Use and Conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: This domain concerns the ability to use written language to convey arguments with clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use proper spelling and grammar; include sentences with a variety of punctuation when comfortable. Avoid repetitive word choices, but also avoid sounding artificial with too many 'big words.' Vary sentence length and structure. Maintain a professional tone—don’t use slang or casual abbreviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test Format and Time Management
rubrics_metrics.description: You will have 40 minutes to complete the writing portion. The test consists of one prompt presenting an issue and three perspectives; all test-takers get the same prompt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the booklet's blank pages for planning (these pages are not scored); only the lined pages you write on are scored. It is recommended to take no more than 10 minutes to plan your essay so you have the rest of the time to write and review it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt Predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: The test is predictable in format and the types of perspectives presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even before reading the prompt you know the format and that the three perspectives are broadly predictable (one will argue in favor, one against, and the third is usually mixed or a different argument). Use this predictability when brainstorming and planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning and Brainstorming (Pro/Con Lists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a pro/con list for each provided perspective after reading the prompt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify strengths and possible counterarguments for each perspective. List concrete examples you could use to support or refute each perspective—use these lists to pick the perspective you can support most effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspective Selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose which perspective to adopt or develop an original one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick the perspective for which you most easily came up with supporting evidence and examples. There is no 'right' answer; graders score the effectiveness of your argument. While you can create an original perspective, unless you have a very clear idea it is advisable to choose one of the three provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis and Outline
rubrics_metrics.description: Write your thesis as a complete sentence and outline the essay before writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to your thesis during planning. Outline with an introduction and conclusion and plan for at least three body paragraphs. Possible outlines: (a) one paragraph for each perspective (start with your perspective then the other two, explaining why each is wrong), or (b) several paragraphs showing multiple ways your perspective is correct and one paragraph explaining why the others are wrong. Use topic sentences and transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing Execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn your outline and brainstorm into the written essay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure your introduction leads to the thesis statement, use topic sentences in body paragraphs, and include transitions when introducing examples and starting/ending paragraphs. Keep the writing focused and coherent with examples tied to claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision and Error Checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-read your essay and correct mistakes before finishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct spelling and grammar mistakes. Double-check for unintentional repetitive words—especially modifiers like 'really' and 'very.' Make final adjustments to clarity and sentence variety as time allows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation Practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer-term preparation activities to improve performance on test day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read and write often across varied styles; pay attention to current events and social issues (Op-Ed pages are recommended). Replicate the testing experience by taking timed practice tests. Get feedback on your writing from teachers, parents, or tutors. Familiarize yourself with the official ACT Writing rubric and study sample essays to understand successful and less successful answers.
